newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen steady at open, quiet until FOMC.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen steady at open, quiet until FOMC.

text.p: Wall Street is seen opening quietly on Tuesday, with most share prices treading water until Federal Reserve policy-makers meeting today announce whether they will boost U.S. short-term interest rates.

The Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy arm, meets starting at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT to discuss U.S. interest rates. Economists are divided as to whether it will take action against inflation by raising the federal funds rate.
Stocks idled on Monday ahead of the meeting, with the Dow industrials ending up 34.21 points at 7228.88 in light trade.
Market-watchers expect more of the same until the FOMC delivers its verdict on rates, expected at around 1415 EDT/1815 GMT.

"I don't see a big move (in stocks) either way," Tom Carpenter, a managing director and chief economist at ASB Capital Management Inc, said. "Everything is on hold until after the 1415 EDT announcement. There is no reason to take a big position ahead of the FOMC results."
At its last meeting in March, the inflation-wary FOMC raised rates for the first time in two years, boosting the key federal funds rate by 25 basis points.
They must now weigh recent data which has shown some softening of the U.S. economy, while searching for any signs of accelerating inflation.
Among its options, the FOMC could let the federal funds rate stand at 5.5 percent, a decision traders and analysts have said could give a lift to the stock market.
Or, it could boost rates by 25 basis points to take a pre-emptive strike against inflation, which might or might not depress stock markets, analysts said.
"Investors will stay on the sideline until we know," said Charlie Crane, market strategist at Key Asset Management.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average shed 156.92 points, or 0.77 percent, to 20,332.83.
In London, the FTSE 100 was off 26.9 points at 4618.3. U.S. stocks were little changed in quiet London trading as European markets waited for the FOMC outcome.
The Standard & Poor's futures index was down 0.85 points at 835.20, and the long bond was flat at a 6.92 percent yield.
The weaker dollar dipped below 113 yen in Tokyo after falling nearly three full yen from its New York close. It was trading at 112.84/89 yen in Tokyo and 1.6972/75 against the mark in Europe.
A softer dollar was seen as mildly supportive for stock markets, analysts said.

"The weaker dollar has been a positive factor in recent weeks," Crane said. "A weaker dollar means stronger dollar-denominated foreign earnings which has lifted the mood of investors looking at the multinationals which populate the Dow and the S&P 500 index."

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said that with so many publicly traded companies trying to capture attention, firms have chosen quirky names. But off-beat names do not always boost the share price.

The New York Times Market Place column said China's stock markets have seen volatile swings of buying and selling, with share prices rising over 60 percent in the first four months of this year before taking a rest.
